opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of progress in architecture research doesn't come from inventing something completely new. It comes from going back to ideas that were dismissed too early and asking *why* they were dismissed. Often the answer is that the idea itself was fine, but the hardware, the scale, or the implementation at the time just couldn't support it.

Linear attention and the delta rule are good examples from my own work. The delta rule is decades old. It goes back to classic work on associative memory and fast weight programmers. People knew it was a more principled way to update a memory than simply adding key-value outer products, because it lets the model correct or overwrite what's stored instead of just piling things up. But for a long time nobody used it at scale, because it looked inherently sequential and you couldn't train it efficiently on GPUs. So it was quietly set aside.

When we revisited it, the key question wasn't "is this a good inductive bias?" We already had reasons to believe it was. The question was "can we make it hardware-efficient?" Once we found a way to parallelize it across the sequence, using chunkwise computation and a compact representation of products of Householder-like matrices, it suddenly became practical. Then DeltaNet and later Gated DeltaNet could actually compete at real scale.

So I see it as a kind of arbitrage. The field moves fast and follows trends, so many techniques get labeled as "doesn't work" when what actually happened was "didn't work under 2015-era constraints." Hardware changes, tensor cores change what's cheap, and our understanding of what matters, like in-context retrieval or state-tracking, changes too. Older ideas deserve a second look under the new conditions.

There's also a deeper reason. Older literature, from online learning, signal processing, and classical RNNs, often has very clean theoretical motivation. Many modern recurrent architectures can be understood as different online learning objectives for updating a memory state. Once you see that unifying view, the old techniques stop being historical curiosities and become a menu of design choices. You can ask which loss the model is optimizing, which optimizer it uses, and how it forgets. That framing came largely from rereading old work.

Finally, I think it's healthy for the community. If everyone only iterates on the current dominant architecture, we get local optimizations. Revisiting neglected ideas keeps the search space wide. Sometimes the old idea turns out to be exactly the missing piece. Even when it isn't, you understand much better why the current approach works.

r001.rationale: The response says the delta rule was set aside and argues for revisiting old ideas, but attributes its neglect to hardware and efficiency constraints, not to a lack of follow-up research.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention Renaissance 2023 or compare its forgetting behavior with earlier techniques.

r003.rationale: It describes progress as going back to ideas dismissed too early and repeatedly urges a second look at older techniques as conditions and understanding change.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think the honest answer is that a lot of what looks like a brand-new idea in architecture research is actually an old idea whose time finally came. When I started working on linear attention and the gated variants, I kept going back to papers from the nineties and early 2000s on recurrent networks, fast weights, associative memory. Those ideas weren't wrong. They were just proposed at a moment when the hardware couldn't make them shine, and then the field moved on and sort of forgot them.

What changed is the hardware and the scale. Today the bottleneck isn't really whether a model can express something, it's whether you can train it efficiently on a GPU at billions of parameters. So an algorithmic trick that got dismissed because it was a bit awkward on a CPU in 1995 can suddenly become the key piece once you ask, "can I write this as a chunkwise matmul and keep the tensor cores busy?" That's exactly the story with things like the delta rule. It's an old online learning update, people treated it as a curiosity, and once you rework it so it's parallelizable it turns into a genuinely competitive sequence model.

The other reason I find this valuable is that it gives you a principled search space instead of random architecture tweaking. When you revisit an old technique, you inherit all the theory and intuition that came with it. You know what it's supposed to be good at, you know where it failed, and that tells you exactly which part needs to be fixed for the modern setting. That's a much better starting point than stacking modules until the loss curve looks nice.

And frankly, it's a way to avoid being trapped by the current dominant paradigm. Transformers are wonderful, but if everyone only iterates on the Transformer, the field converges on local improvements. Looking back at neglected ideas is a cheap way to inject some diversity into what we're exploring, and sometimes one of those old ideas, combined with today's engineering, turns out to be the thing that moves the frontier.

r001.rationale: The response says the field moved on and forgot earlier ideas, but does not identify a lack of follow-up research as the reason they remained overlooked.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Renaissance 2023 or compare its forgetting mechanism with techniques from earlier research.

r003.rationale: The response describes revisiting older ideas, but does not characterize algorithmic progress as a recurring spiral that repeatedly returns to earlier techniques.

astra-6.text:
I think an algorithm can be neglected because it was a poor fit for the hardware of its time, rather than because the underlying idea was weak. As hardware changes, those tradeoffs change. A technique that once looked too expensive might become attractive if it reduces data movement or exposes more parallelism.

Revisiting those ideas also helps us question the assumptions behind current architectures. Instead of only asking how to make today’s popular algorithms run faster, we can ask what kinds of computation a different architecture could make practical. That gives us a broader space to explore. The important thing is to understand why a technique was set aside and test whether that reason still holds.

r001.rationale: The response attributes neglect to poor fit with past hardware, but does not identify a lack of follow-up research.

r002.rationale: It does not mention Renaissance 2023 or compare its forgetting with techniques in earlier research.

r003.rationale: It supports revisiting neglected ideas, but does not characterize algorithmic progress as a spiral that repeatedly revisits earlier techniques.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s valuable because an algorithm is always judged within a particular hardware context. A technique that looked inefficient years ago might become attractive when the balance between computation, memory access, and communication changes.

Revisiting those techniques gives us a chance to question assumptions we’ve inherited. Was the idea fundamentally limited, or was it simply a poor fit for the machines available at the time? Sometimes a small change in the algorithm makes it work well on today’s hardware. Sometimes the algorithm reveals what we should change in the architecture.

That interaction is where I think a lot of interesting research happens. We’re not just trying to run an existing workload faster; we’re exploring whether a different way of expressing the computation opens up better design choices.

r001.rationale: It discusses revisiting older techniques and inherited assumptions, but does not identify a lack of follow-up research as the reason techniques remain overlooked.

r002.rationale: The response says nothing about Renaissance 2023 or comparing its forgetting granularity with earlier research.

r003.rationale: It describes revisiting past techniques, but does not characterize algorithmic progress as a spiraling process that repeatedly cycles back to them.
